'You'll come to the ghat at dawn?' Ganga asked, folding the new sari for the Chhath puja.
'Of course, Maa. I'll carry the soop.'
'Even though you don't believe any of it now.'
Tushar sat beside her. 'I believe in you standing in cold water for all of us every year. That's reason enough to carry the basket.'
From the kitchen, Bua called, 'Tushar, you'll fast too, na?'
'No, Bua. But I'll make sure everyone who's fasting gets home warm.'
'Arre, what kind of...'
'Leave him,' Ganga said. 'He has never once laughed at our puja. Not once.'
Bua grumbled but went back to the thekua.
Ganga squeezed his hand. 'I used to lie awake worrying about this.'
'And now?'
'Now I just worry you'll drop the soop.'
He laughed. 'Only if you make me carry the sugarcane too.'

When Leela moved into her new flat last month, she invited me to the griha pravesh puja, a little nervously. Two years ago we would have argued all evening. I was newly Buddhist then, and I thought I had to prove something every time I opened my mouth.
This time I went early and helped her carry the kalash over the threshold. I sat quietly through the whole puja. When her in-laws asked about my meditation retreat, I answered what they asked, and nothing more.
Later, washing plates together, Leela said, 'You didn't make one sarcastic comment, Chetan.' I told her I didn't have any. Her faith is hers; my practice is mine. We both still care about the same things: our parents, honesty, feeding whoever turns up.
I didn't win anything that day. It felt much better than winning.

qa.q: What did Chetan help Leela carry over the threshold?
qa.a: Chetan helped her carry the kalash.

qa.q: Why was Leela a little nervous when inviting Chetan?
qa.a: She likely remembered their old arguments and worried that Chetan might criticise the puja in front of everyone.

qa.q: What changed in how Chetan handles their different beliefs?
qa.a: Chetan now joins the puja respectfully, answers questions without preaching and focuses on shared values instead of proving a point.

qa.q: How might Leela's in-laws have experienced Chetan at the puja?
qa.a: They probably found Chetan respectful and easy to talk to, answering their questions plainly and sitting quietly through the ritual.

grounding: It shows someone on a different spiritual path keeping close family ties, joining a ritual respectfully and choosing peace over winning.

Family counsellor's note, after final session
Mohit first came to me a year ago. He had stopped believing in his family's faith, and every visit home turned into a shouting match with his father about rituals.
This month I met the family after his sister Alka's wedding. His mother described what happened. Mohit sat through the whole ceremony, let the priest tie the red thread on his wrist, and carried the heavy puja tray for his grandmother, who couldn't manage the stairs. He didn't pretend to believe; when an uncle asked, he said simply, "I'm here for Alka." He also didn't make a single joke about the rituals, which Alka said she had been dreading.
His father told me, "We don't agree. But he was there for us."
Mohit said peace came when he stopped trying to win. We agreed this would be our last session.

qa.q: What did Mohit carry for his grandmother?
qa.a: The heavy puja tray.

qa.q: What does Mohit's line 'I'm here for Alka' reveal about his feelings?
qa.a: He feels love for his sister and calm about his own beliefs, joining the ritual for affection, not creed.

qa.q: What choices helped Mohit find peace with his family?
qa.a: He joined rituals out of love, was honest when asked, didn't mock belief, and stopped trying to win arguments.

qa.q: How does Mohit's father see him now?
qa.a: His father still disagrees but feels grateful and respected, seeing that Mohit showed up for the family.

grounding: A counsellor notes a young man who keeps family ties, joins rituals out of love rather than creed, and neither mocks nor pressures.

25 December, Aizawl
Went to the Christmas service with Nu and Pa this morning. I haven't believed the way they do for three years now, and they know. But I wore the new puan Nu wove for me and sat between them, and I sang every carol, because those songs are my childhood and my mother's voice.
I didn't take communion. Nobody made a fuss. Pa squeezed my shoulder when the choir sang his favourite hymn.
Last year I'd have argued with my cousin over lunch when he started on about sinners. This year I just asked about his new baby. It's not that I've gone soft. I just don't need to win any more.
Sabina called in the evening to wish me; she's in Delhi with her family for the holidays. She laughed and said, "Look at us. A Muslim wishing an ex-believer Merry Christmas." It felt exactly right.
Lalremsiami

qa.a: The new puan Nu wove.

qa.a: Lalremsiami felt love and nostalgia, since the songs carry childhood and a mother's voice.

passage: In Gurleen's village near Moga, the whole lane was busy for the gurpurab langar. Gurleen had not believed in much for years now, and her family knew it. Still, she was up at five, rolling rotis with her aunts in the gurdwara's kitchen, her head covered, laughing at her Taiji's gossip. Her husband Francis, who had grown up Catholic in Goa, stirred the huge pot of dal and asked her uncle endless questions about the recipe. When her cousin teased, "Our atheist is the fastest roti-maker," Gurleen just grinned. "Somebody has to be." Later, sitting in a row on the floor, eating from the same steel plates, her Biji squeezed her hand. Gurleen didn't bow her head for the ardas, but she stood quietly through it. She had come for love of these people, and that was enough for everyone in the room.
